name: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
title: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
answer: This page covers the accounting treatment and valuation methods for digital tokens that do not trade on an active market, including locked, restricted, and low-volume assets. It addresses how to measure fair value when observable prices are absent or unreliable, and how to distinguish between cost, impairment, and revaluation models. The focus is on tokens held by companies, funds, and treasuries rather than personal holdings.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the accounting treatment and valuation methods for digital tokens that do not trade on an active market, including locked, restricted, and low-volume assets. It addresses how to measure fair value when observable prices are absent or unreliable, and how to distinguish between cost, impairment, and revaluation models. The focus is on tokens held by companies, funds, and treasuries rather than personal holdings.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Valuation work relies on on-chain transaction data, order book snapshots from decentralized exchanges, and token unlock schedules pulled from smart contracts or custody reports. These inputs feed into internal valuation models, often maintained in spreadsheets or accounting software, with separate storage for supporting evidence such as last-round pricing and comparable token sales. No single market data feed is sufficient for illiquid tokens, so the infrastructure must combine several sources and flag stale or thin data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work typically follows a fair value hierarchy, starting with quoted prices in active markets and moving to observable inputs such as recent private transactions or comparable token prices, then to unobservable inputs like discounted cash flow from expected token utility. Common techniques include a market approach using last financing round price adjusted for liquidity and vesting, an income approach based on projected protocol fees or token demand, and an option-pricing model for locked tokens with time-based restrictions. Valuers often apply a discount for lack of marketability and document the key assumptions behind each input.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on the provenance of pricing data and the defensibility of assumptions, since auditors and regulators may challenge valuations that rely on thin or self-reported trading. There is a risk of manipulation in low-liquidity markets, and token lockups or transfer restrictions can create a gap between nominal value and realizable value. Good practice requires an independent review of models, clear documentation of data sources, and separation between those who originate a token position and those who value it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more standardized valuation frameworks as accounting bodies and auditors publish guidance for digital assets, and as tokenized traditional assets bring more observable pricing. Automated valuation models that ingest on-chain data and apply machine learning to detect comparable transactions are likely to reduce manual effort, though human judgment will remain for unobservable inputs. Expect greater emphasis on audit trails, model validation, and real-time impairment testing as illiquid token holdings become more common on balance sheets.
